questions.question: What is the difference between Authentication and Authorization in Spring Security?
questions.title: Authentication vs Authorization in Spring Security
questions.direct_answer: **Authentication** answers "Who are you?" — verifies identity by checking credentials and produces an `Authentication` object stored in the **`SecurityContext`**. **Authorization** answers "What are you allowed to do?" — checks the principal's `GrantedAuthority` collection against required permissions for a resource. Spring enforces them as **two distinct, sequential steps**: `AuthenticationManager` first, then `AuthorizationManager` (or `@PreAuthorize`). The clearest signal that you understand the difference: **401 means unauthenticated; 403 means authenticated-but-unauthorized** — never return 403 to anonymous requests, it leaks resource existence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can clearly articulate the two-step security model and map it to Spring Security's concrete types.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Conflating the two concepts, or not knowing that Authorization can only work after Authentication populates the SecurityContext.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference the Authentication interface, GrantedAuthority, AuthenticationManager, and AccessDecisionManager (or the newer AuthorizationManager in Spring Security 6).

sections.title: Two Sequential Steps: WHO Then WHAT
sections.content:
The two concepts are **sequential** — authentication must happen before authorization can work. You cannot decide what a user is allowed to do until you know who they are. Conflating them is the most common mistake in security interviews and leads to real bugs (returning 403 to anonymous users tells attackers the resource exists).

In Spring, **authentication** is handled by `AuthenticationManager`, delegating to one or more `AuthenticationProvider` implementations. The result is an **`Authentication`** object in `SecurityContextHolder` carrying three things: **principal** (who), **credentials** (proof, usually cleared after success), and a collection of **`GrantedAuthority`** (roles and permissions).

**Authorization** uses those `GrantedAuthority` values to make access decisions.
- **`AuthorizationManager`** (which replaced `AccessDecisionManager` in Spring Security 6) evaluates whether the principal holds the required authority.
- Authorization happens at two layers: **URL-level** (filter chain via `requestMatchers().hasRole()`) — fast and coarse, and **method-level** (`@PreAuthorize` with SpEL) — fine-grained, can inspect arguments and return values.

**401 vs 403** is the clearest test: 401 means "I don't know who you are"; 403 means "I know you, but no." Spring handles this correctly by default — `AuthenticationEntryPoint` sends 401, `AccessDeniedHandler` sends 403.

sections.title: Authentication vs Authorization: Components and Behavior
sections.content:
The distinction maps directly to different Spring Security components.

| Aspect | Authentication | Authorization |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | Who are you? | What can you do? |
| **When** | First — before any access decision | After — requires authenticated principal |
| **Failure response** | 401 Unauthorized | 403 Forbidden |
| **Spring component** | `AuthenticationManager` / `AuthenticationProvider` | `AuthorizationManager` / `@PreAuthorize` |
| **Data produced** | `Authentication` object (principal + credentials) | Access decision (allow or deny) |
| **Input** | Credentials (username/password, token, certificate) | `GrantedAuthority` collection + required permission |
| **Storage** | `SecurityContextHolder` (ThreadLocal per request) | Evaluated per request — not stored |
| **Configuration** | `UserDetailsService`, OAuth2, LDAP, SAML | `requestMatchers().hasRole()`, `@PreAuthorize` |

**`GrantedAuthority` is the bridge** between phases. Roles attached during authentication become the vocabulary authorization rules consume. A `GrantedAuthority` of `ROLE_ADMIN` attached during login is what makes `hasRole("ADMIN")` return true later.

**Common bug:** if roles aren't attached correctly during authentication, every authorization check fails — and the symptom looks like a broken authorization rule when the actual bug is in the authentication phase.

sections.title: URL-Level vs Method-Level Authorization
sections.content:
**URL-level authorization (filter chain):**
- `requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")`
- Applies to entire endpoint groups, runs at the filter layer before any application code
- Fastest line of defense — obviously unauthorized requests rejected before consuming app resources
- Coarse-grained — limited to URL patterns

**Method-level authorization (annotations):**
- `@PreAuthorize`, `@PostAuthorize` — fine-grained rules with domain-data dependencies
- Example: "only the owner can delete their post" can't be expressed as a URL
- `@PreAuthorize("#post.authorId == authentication.principal.id")` — accesses method parameters
- Slightly slower (SpEL evaluation per call); needs Spring AOP proxies

**Use both layers together:**
- URL rules reject obvious cases early
- Method-level enforces ownership and attribute-based checks
- Common mistake: relying only on URL rules — one wildcard misconfig exposes the API
- Defense in depth — `@PreAuthorize` is a second check even if URL is misconfigured

**Practical pattern:**
- Configure URL rules broadly (`authenticated()`)
- Enforce specific role and ownership constraints with method annotations
- Separates authentication enforcement (URL) from authorization logic (method)
- Both easier to audit and test independently

sections.title: Authorization Architecture: When and What to Watch
sections.content:
**When URL-level helps:**
- Coarse role-based gating (admin vs user areas)
- Public/private endpoint separation
- Pre-flight rejection of unauthorized requests (saves CPU)
- Centralized in `SecurityFilterChain` — easy to audit

**When method-level helps:**
- Resource ownership (post owner, order customer)
- Attribute-based access (department, tenant, plan tier)
- Post-execution filtering (`@PostAuthorize`, `@PostFilter`)
- Service-layer reuse from multiple entry points (REST + GraphQL + scheduled jobs)

**When it hurts:**
- Complex SpEL expressions become unmaintainable — extract to `@authService.canAccess(...)`
- Method security on `private` or self-invoked methods silently does nothing (AOP)
- URL rules ignored on resources behind a forwarder/proxy that bypasses the filter chain
- Returning 403 to unauthenticated users leaks resource existence

**Watch for:**
- **`@EnableMethodSecurity`** must be on a `@Configuration` class — without it `@PreAuthorize` is silently ignored
- **Self-invocation** bypasses AOP — `this.securedMethod()` inside the same class skips the security proxy
- **`hasRole("ADMIN")` vs `hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")`** — `hasRole()` auto-prepends `ROLE_`; mismatched expectations break checks
- **CORS preflight (OPTIONS)** must be permitted before authorization — otherwise browsers see 401 and never retry
- **Test both 401 (unauthenticated) and 403 (wrong role) paths** for every protected endpoint

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Authentication answers 'who?'; authorization answers 'what?'** — auth must succeed before authz; 401 = unauthenticated, 403 = authenticated but unauthorized.
- **`Authentication` object holds the principal and authorities** — stored in `SecurityContext`; `getAuthorities()` returns `GrantedAuthority` checked by authorization.
- **`AuthenticationManager` delegates to `AuthenticationProvider` chain** — `DaoAuthenticationProvider` is default; loads `UserDetails` and verifies password with `PasswordEncoder`.
- **Authorization runs after authentication in the filter chain** — `AuthorizationFilter` (or `FilterSecurityInterceptor`) follows the auth filter; can't authorize before identity is known.
- **`@PreAuthorize` is a second layer to URL rules** — defense in depth; HTTP rules protect endpoints, method annotations protect service methods.
- **`AuthorizationManager` replaced `AccessDecisionManager`** in Spring Security 6 — cleaner architecture, lambda-based.
- **CORS preflight must be `permitAll`** — or browsers see 401 on OPTIONS and never retry the real request.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Authentication — identity verification**
- 'Who are you?' — user presents credentials (password, JWT, certificate)
- `AuthenticationManager` verifies
- On success: `Authentication` object stored in `SecurityContextHolder` with principal + `GrantedAuthority` list
- Failure: `AuthenticationException` -> 401

**Authorization — permission check**
- 'What can you do?' — evaluated after authentication succeeds
- Spring checks `GrantedAuthority` against required permission
- Failure: `AccessDeniedException` -> 403

**The Spring Security flow**
- Request enters filter chain
- Auth filter (e.g., `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`) extracts credentials, calls `AuthenticationManager`
- `DaoAuthenticationProvider` loads `UserDetails` via `UserDetailsService`, verifies password
- On success: stores `Authentication` in `SecurityContextHolder`
- `AuthorizationFilter` checks against required authorities for the URL

**Method security (`@PreAuthorize`)**
- Adds a second authorization layer on service methods
- Even if HTTP-level check is bypassed, method-level still enforces
- SpEL access to parameters, principal, and Spring beans

**Common pitfalls**
- Returning 403 instead of 401 for anonymous users (leaks resource existence)
- Forgetting `@EnableMethodSecurity` -> `@PreAuthorize` silently does nothing
- Self-invocation skips AOP -> method-level security bypassed
- CORS preflight OPTIONS rejected because not `permitAll` -> entire API breaks for browsers

questions.question: What are the differences between @PreAuthorize, @Secured, and @RolesAllowed in Spring Security?
questions.title: @PreAuthorize vs @Secured vs @RolesAllowed
questions.direct_answer: **`@PreAuthorize`** is the most powerful — accepts **SpEL** and can inspect method arguments, return values, and Spring beans (`@authService.canAccess(#id, authentication)`). **`@Secured`** accepts a list of role strings only and predates SpEL. **`@RolesAllowed`** is the **JSR-250** standard, also role-string only. For any non-trivial logic — ownership, parameter checks, custom evaluators — **`@PreAuthorize` is the modern default**. Combine with **`@PostAuthorize`** for return-value checks and **`@PreFilter`/`@PostFilter`** for collection element filtering. Enable with **`@EnableMethodSecurity`** in Spring Security 6 (replaces deprecated `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity`).

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of method security options and when to use SpEL expressions vs simple role checks.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Secured or @RolesAllowed and then discovering they cannot express 'only the owner of this resource can edit it' — that requires SpEL in @PreAuthorize.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @PostAuthorize for filtering return values, @PreFilter/@PostFilter for collections, and that method security requires @EnableMethodSecurity (not @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6).

sections.title: @Secured Can't Express Ownership; @PreAuthorize Can
sections.content:
Most developers start with `@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")` because it looks clean.
- Then the requirement arrives: "only the owner can edit their order.
- **`@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed` cannot express this** — they accept role strings and check membership, nothing more.
- Resource-level authorization that depends on the relationship between the user and the data is impossible.

**`@PreAuthorize`** accepts **SpEL** with access to method parameters, the principal, and Spring beans. `@PreAuthorize("#order.userId == authentication.principal.id")` checks ownership. `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or @orderService.isOwner(#orderId, authentication)")` combines role + bean call. The **`@orderService` bean call** is the key capability — any authorization logic can be a Spring bean method invoked from SpEL.

The migration from `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity` (deprecated in Spring 6) to **`@EnableMethodSecurity`** is required for new code.
- The new annotation enables `@PreAuthorize` by default and uses the cleaner `AuthorizationManager` architecture.
- **Getting this wrong means `@PreAuthorize` silently has no effect** — no exception, all access permitted.
- Always test method security annotations.

sections.title: Three Annotations Compared
sections.content:
The decision matrix is straightforward once you know what each can express.

| Aspect | @Secured | @RolesAllowed | @PreAuthorize |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Standard** | Spring-specific | JSR-250 (Jakarta EE) | Spring-specific |
| **SpEL expressions** | No | No | Yes — full SpEL |
| **Role checks** | Yes | Yes | Yes — `hasRole()`, `hasAuthority()` |
| **Parameter access** | No | No | Yes — `#paramName` |
| **Principal access** | No | No | Yes — `authentication.principal.id` |
| **Custom beans** | No | No | Yes — `@beanName.method()` |
| **Post-execution filter** | No | No | Yes — `@PostAuthorize`, `@PostFilter` |
| **Enable with** | `@EnableMethodSecurity(securedEnabled=true)` | `@EnableMethodSecurity(jsr250Enabled=true)` | `@EnableMethodSecurity` (default on) |
| **Spring Security 6 status** | Supported | Supported | Preferred |

**`@PostAuthorize`** evaluates after the method runs and can access `returnObject`. `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.userId == authentication.principal.id")` ensures `findById()` doesn't return another user's data — method runs, but result blocked if condition fails.

**`@PreFilter` / `@PostFilter`** apply to collections — `@PreFilter` removes input elements that don't satisfy the expression before the method runs; `@PostFilter` removes output elements after. Powerful for **multi-tenant** apps where every user should see only their own data.

sections.title: Decision Guide: When to Reach for Each
sections.content:
**Use `@PreAuthorize` for everything new:**
- Covers every case `@Secured`/`@RolesAllowed` cover, plus more
- Resource ownership, parameter-based access, post-execution filtering
- Only reason to use `@Secured`/`@RolesAllowed`: codebase consistency

**Simple role checks:**
- `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` is slightly more verbose than `@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")`
- But provides consistent pattern — reviewers don't switch contexts

**`hasRole` vs `hasAuthority` — important distinction:**
- `hasRole('ADMIN')` automatically prepends `ROLE_` -> looks for `ROLE_ADMIN`
- `hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN')` checks the exact string
- For custom authorities without `ROLE_` prefix (e.g., `READ_REPORTS`), use `hasAuthority`

**Complex SpEL — extract to a service:**
- `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('MANAGER') and @projectService.isTeamMember(#projectId, authentication) and @planLimits.withinQuota(authentication)")` is unmaintainable
- Better: `@PreAuthorize("@authService.canAccess(#projectId, authentication)")`
- Logic becomes unit-testable independently
- Can use a `PermissionEvaluator` for `hasPermission(#id, 'PROJECT', 'READ')` style

**Enable with `@EnableMethodSecurity`:**
- On any `@Configuration` class
- `prePostEnabled=true` no longer needed — default in Spring 6
- Add `securedEnabled=true` or `jsr250Enabled=true` only if migrating legacy annotations

sections.title: Method Security: Helps, Hurts, Watch For
sections.content:
**When @PreAuthorize helps:**
- Resource ownership rules
- Multi-tenant isolation
- Reusing security logic across REST, GraphQL, scheduled jobs
- Combining roles with attribute-based decisions

**When @PostAuthorize/@PostFilter help:**
- Authorization that depends on the result (you don't know the owner until you load it)
- Filtering search results to elements the user is allowed to see
- Defense against accidental data leak in lookup methods

**When it hurts:**
- Complex SpEL becomes a code smell — extract to a bean
- `@PostFilter` on huge collections is expensive — page-size matters
- AOP proxies are bypassed by `private`, `final`, or self-invoked methods
- Method-only enforcement without HTTP rules -> attackers can probe before authentication

**Watch for:**
- **Self-invocation trap** — `this.securedMethod()` skips AOP; inject self via interface or use `AspectJ` mode
- **`@EnableMethodSecurity` placement** — must be on a `@Configuration` class loaded by the context; `@WebMvcTest` may not load it
- **`hasRole` vs `hasAuthority`** — silent mismatches
- **Authentication can be null** — `authentication == null` in SpEL crashes; prefer `isAuthenticated()` first
- **Test both branches** — `@WithMockUser(roles="USER")` for the deny path, `@WithMockUser(roles="ADMIN")` for the allow path
- **Spring Security 6 default `AuthorizationManager`** — old voter-based code that customized `AccessDecisionManager` needs migration

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@PreAuthorize` supports SpEL; `@Secured`/`@RolesAllowed` do not** — `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #userId == authentication.name")` uses parameters in expression.
- **`@EnableMethodSecurity` replaces `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity`** in Spring Security 6.x; old annotation is deprecated.
- **`@PostAuthorize` evaluates after method returns** — check ownership: `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")`.
- **`@PreFilter`/`@PostFilter` filter collections** — `@PreFilter("filterObject.userId == authentication.name")` removes elements user doesn't own.
- **Method security uses AOP proxies — self-invocation bypasses it** — `this.securedMethod()` inside the same class skips the security proxy.
- **`hasRole('ADMIN')` adds `ROLE_` prefix; `hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN')` is exact** — choose deliberately based on your authority naming.
- **Extract complex SpEL into a bean method** — `@authService.canAccess(...)` is testable; long inline SpEL is not.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**`@PreAuthorize` — the standard choice**
- `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` — simple role check
- `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('USER') and #id == authentication.name")` — `#id` references method parameter
- `@PreAuthorize("@authService.canAccess(#id, authentication)")` — invoke a Spring bean
- Evaluated before method runs

**`@PostAuthorize` — for ownership checks on return values**
- `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")`
- Method runs first, then expression evaluates against return
- Use when you can't determine authorization without the result

**`@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed`**
- `@Secured({"ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_MANAGER"})` — Spring-specific; role strings only
- `@RolesAllowed("ADMIN")` — JSR-250; Java standard; role strings only
- No SpEL — use `@PreAuthorize` for anything beyond a simple role list

**`@PreFilter` / `@PostFilter`**
- `@PreFilter("filterObject.userId == authentication.name")` — remove input elements user doesn't own
- `@PostFilter("filterObject.public or filterObject.userId == authentication.name")` — filter results
- Powerful for multi-tenant data isolation

**Self-invocation trap**
- AOP-based; `this.method()` bypasses the proxy
- Always inject the bean and call through proxy for method security to work

**Enable**
- `@EnableMethodSecurity` in Spring Security 6
- Replaces deprecated `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity`
- `@PreAuthorize` enabled by default; `securedEnabled=true` / `jsr250Enabled=true` opt-in
